description: We’re a team of engineering and technology enthusiasts interested in AI, computer vision, software development, data visualization, and space technology. We enjoy learning by building and solving real-world problems. We’re looking for motivated teammates with skills in AI/ML, computer vision, web development, astronomy, UI/UX, data visualization, or research. Curiosity and willingness to learn matter most!
summary:
SPHEREx Sky Explorer is an interactive public web platform that allows astronomers and citizen scientists to enter or click any sky coordinate (RA/Dec) and investigate how that patch of sky evolves over time across SPHEREx's 102 infrared spectral channels (0.75–5.00 µm). Guided by the design principle "The Map locates; the Lab analyzes," the application combines an Aladin Lite v3 sky atlas (featuring Sesame object resolution, Gaia DR3 overlays, and optional SPHEREx DR1 HiPS cube slice scrubbing) with a high-speed browser Analysis Lab.

Because SPHEREx uses Linear Variable Filters, every pixel samples a distinct wavelength while fast-moving objects shift across ~6-month revisits. Our Python pipeline performs epoch-aware IRSA TAP discovery (dr1 and qr3), subtracts zodiacal light, masks 15 bad-data flag bits, reprojects cutouts onto a north-up 6.15"/pixel TAN grid, and cross-checks motion against ESA Gaia DR3. Compact IEEE 754 float16 binary cubes stream to the browser for instant matched-wavelength blinking, temporal/spectral difference imaging, inverse-variance false-color RGB mixing, and λ–time spectrophotometry.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

SPHEREx Sky Explorer turns Multi-Extension FITS spectral cutouts into an interactive time-domain workspace. A unified Python pipeline serves both pre-computed zero-latency showcases (Tier 1 targets: Barnard's Star, WISE 0855, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis; Tier 1.5 IRSA tutorial fields: M101, COSMOS, intro, and HiPS positions) and live on-demand coordinate jobs (Tier 2) via POST /api/jobs and Server-Sent Events (GET /api/jobs/{id}/events).

During discovery, the backend queries IRSA TAP (https://irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/TAP) using ADQL 2.0 across releases dr1 and qr3, deduplicates by newest processing version, and propagates target coordinates (α(t), δ(t)) to each exposure's timestamp so high-proper-motion objects like WISE 0855 (≈ -8.12"/yr RA) remain centered. Each cutout undergoes zodiacal-light and local sigma-clipped background subtraction (I' = IMAGE - ZODI - B), bitmask filtering (BAD_MASK = 712439, preserving benign SOURCE bit 21), and reprojection onto a north-up 6.15"/pixel TAN grid (60 × 60 pixels for a 0.1° field).

In the browser Analysis Lab, users explore five tools:

1. Time Slider (Blink): Clusters frames into epochs (epoch_gap_days = 30), steps through matching wavelength windows (|λ - λ₀| < bandwidth), overlays Gaia predicted tracks, and color-codes slider ticks by frame contamination.

2. Difference Imaging: Computes temporal (same detector/wavelength, different epochs) and spectral signal-to-noise difference maps (S = D / σ_D with ±3σ marching-squares contours) to isolate moving dipoles and variable stars.

3. False-Color RGB Compositor: Mixes inverse-variance weighted coadds client-side with asinh stretching across Detector RGB, Equal-Channel RGB, Feature RGB (continuum-subtracted maps around 8 spectral lines including Paα, 3.3 µm PAH, and Brα), and custom channel assignments.

4. SED & λ–Time Plane: Extracts forced aperture photometry (3, 4, and 5 px radii with a 6–10 px background annulus) converted from MJy/sr to mJy, displaying spectra and light curves side by side with hollow flagged points and a hatched dichroic gap (channels 50–51).

5. Gaia DR3 Cross-Check: Queries gaiadr3.gaia_source via ESA TAP, fits weighted linear centroids across SPHEREx epochs, and classifies targets within 3σ as match_consistent, match_inconsistent, or no_counterpart.

Tools, Languages & Technologies Used

- Frontend: TypeScript 5, React 18, Vite 5, Tailwind CSS 3, Zustand, Aladin Lite v3 (3.7.0), HTML5 Canvas 2D, SVG (d3-scale, d3-array, d3-format), Vitest, and Playwright.

- Backend & Data Processing: Python (FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, Astropy, Astroquery, PyVO, Photutils, Reproject, NumPy), ADQL 2.0, and JSON Schema v1.0.0 validation.

Creativity & Engineering Factors Considered

- Zero-CORS Backend Proxy: All IRSA and ESA queries execute server-side in Python, protecting the browser from undocumented CORS behavior and rate limits while bounding concurrent downloads with an 8-worker semaphore, 3 retries (10n s backoff), and a backfill pass.

- Compact float16 Binary Cubes: Exporting intensity and 1σ uncertainty as little-endian IEEE 754 float16 arrays (frames.bin, ~3.6 MB for 500 frames at 60 × 60 px) enables <16 ms frame blinking and instant client-side stretch/RGB updates without network refetching.

- Resilience & Accessibility: Startup Gate G1 probes Aladin Lite HiPS cube support with automatic fallback to standard sky layers, file transfers are verified via byte-length and SHA-256 hashes, and visuals use color-blind-safe Okabe-Ito palettes paired with shape cues and full keyboard/ARIA support.

Intended Impact

SPHEREx Sky Explorer lowers the barrier to multi-epoch infrared spectrophotometry, empowering both researchers and citizen scientists to discover brown dwarfs, blended multiples, and variable stars directly in a web browser—with a v2 roadmap to integrate Canadian Space Agency (CSA) NEOSSat and CADC observations for near-Earth asteroid and orbital debris tracking.
